user_statement: There is no rocking our play, it takes some small amount of force to get the joints to connect, but it is possible, and the friction fit is tight. The keeper inserts, and I suppose that is the lock, but the little tiny bit on the keeper is incredibly flimsy, no tension at all at that size. I would say that the friction fit of all pieces (both the two interlocking halves as they slide together and the keeper itself into that final slot) is many orders of magnitude more force than what that tiny bit provides, and that is true, but also we are talking 0 tension at all on the tiny bit.

observations.assembly_force_description: Small force required; tight friction fit.
observations.keeper_catch_description: Very flimsy with essentially zero observed spring tension; retention is dominated by friction.
observations.user_suspected_contributor: Short X extent of some joint components; longer X engagement suggested for investigation.

decision: The complete joint is under redesign for simple assembly. Neither coupon half is selected for reuse. The faucet display cover is the preferred physically proven example for simple, broad-wall snap retention.
limits: Observed tight fit and no play do not establish design acceptance, measured force or full-width carrier stiffness. The tiny keeper catch provides no meaningful observed spring tension.
assembly_acceptance: Two mating halves assemble and retain themselves in the normal seating motion; no separate keeper or extra fastening step. Simpler assembly is a required benefit of the snap fit.
user_assembly_priority: Half the value of moving to snap fit is simpler assembly; a separate keeper does not supply that benefit.
user_design_feedback: Please don’t consider that “it fit well” reason to use that design or any part of it. Please consider I prefer simplicity and the previous design and the remaining half still seem overly complicated to me. Please consider I don’t love the nameplate for its complexity, and the faucet display cover is the only one that has been simple enough, with thick enough and broad enough components for the snap.
additional_user_statement: On that last joint, that test coupon with the keeper. I wanted to also mention, that once assembled, the pieces are rock solid, but there is bending/bowing in the X axis more easily than I would like for the function of this tee carrier. I can see how increasing the X length of some aspects might improve the situation, but wanted to mention only that the short x distance of some of those components lends itself to bending too easily in that direction.
stiffness_status: Physically observed coupon bending is excessive for the intended carrier function. Secure joint fit is not assembled stiffness acceptance; load magnitude and bending mode remain unmeasured.
